attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, in his own voice.

semantics.note: Faithful. It keeps 'a problem' (not 'the main problem') and the 'often' qualifier. It describes the state of things at the time, so observation is the right kind.

contract.note: The plain reading (unusual road situations were a recurring practical difficulty, not that most trips failed) is fair and ordinary. Using the publication month up to the post date is reasonable. The contract correctly declines to infer a specific ML cause.

evidence.note: San Francisco's NHTSA filing of Aug 17, 2023 describes ongoing Cruise trouble recognising construction cones and signs, including the Aug 8 stop and the Aug 15 wet-concrete incident. It falls within the period.

The Aug 7, 2023 CPUC presentation by SF fire, police and transportation officials names recurring perception problems with caution tape, cones, wires and human traffic control. It falls within the period.

reviews.rationale: Two official filings from the period document recurring difficulty with unusual road situations, such as construction zones, emergency scenes and human traffic control. That meets the support condition. No representative evaluation shows these difficulties had gone away. The claim's ML mechanism is not isolated, but the plain-reading contract does not require it to be.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, in his own voice.

semantics.note: This is an unbounded, aphoristic generalisation: no matter how much data, there is always something new. It is a quip about the long tail after the concrete incident, not a datable observation. The drafter's wording 'will always' also turns it into an unlimited forecast. Neither version can be tested.

contract.note: The contract shrinks an unlimited 'always' to one week, which the speaker never supplied. It also requires proprietary training-coverage audits that his words do not invoke. That reading is stretched rather than ordinary.

evidence.note: The Register (Aug 16, 2023) reports the Cruise wet-concrete incident. It establishes an unusual event but says nothing about training coverage.
A 2021 Waymo blog post about simulating rare scenarios. It is a company disclosure from outside the period and about a different company. It does not contradict the claim.

reviews.rationale: The statement is a sweeping, unfalsifiable generalisation that new situations will always arise however much training data is used. No dated evidence could confirm or refute 'always'. The one-week contract is the evaluator's construction, not the speaker's. Even under that contract, the packet has no training-coverage evidence. The claim is not scored.
